lead: C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> is the extra heat per kelvin a substance needs at constant pressure, because it also expands against its surroundings. The difference follows from the equation of state through two PVT derivatives: the thermal expansion coefficient α and the isothermal compressibility κ<sub>T</sub>. Second derivatives of the equation of state then give how C<sub>P</sub> and C<sub>V</sub> change with pressure and volume, and the ratio γ = C<sub>P</sub>/C<sub>V</sub> follows. These relations turn table data into heat capacities for liquids and real gases.
prereq: You need the Maxwell relations of Maxwell relations, the coefficient identities of fundamental property relations, heat capacities from the first-law chapters and equations of state from the PVT-behaviour chapters.

blocks.text: At constant volume, heat raises internal energy only. At constant pressure, heat also pays for expansion work and for pulling the molecules apart. So C<sub>P</sub> ≥ C<sub>V</sub>, with equality only when α = 0, as for liquid water at about 4 °C, where its density is greatest. The gap depends on how fast volume grows with temperature and how hard the fluid is to compress.
Let v be molar volume in m³ mol⁻¹, T temperature in K, α thermal expansion coefficient in K⁻¹, and κ<sub>T</sub> isothermal compressibility in Pa⁻¹.
Cp − Cv = T v α² / κ<sub>T</sub> = −T (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>² / (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>
blocks.where: Cp and Cv are molar heat capacities in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; α = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)<sub>P</sub>; κ<sub>T</sub> = −(1/v)(∂v/∂P)<sub>T</sub>.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas α = 1/T and κ<sub>T</sub> = 1/P. Substitution gives Cp − Cv = R, where R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items: Read T and v from the problem.
Look up α and κ<sub>T</sub> in tables.
Compute Tvα²/κ<sub>T</sub> in consistent SI units.

blocks.text: For liquids α is small and κ<sub>T</sub> is very small, so C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> is only about 1 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water, not R. For a dense gas the difference rises above R, as worked example 2 shows for CO<sub>2</sub>.

sections.h3: Ratio and pressure or volume dependence

blocks.text: Define γ = Cp/Cv. For ideal monatomic gas γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67; for ideal diatomic gas γ = 7/5 = 1.40 at ordinary temperature.
Heat capacities are not truly constant. Their slopes come from second derivatives of the equation of state:

blocks.where: v is molar volume; the derivative is at fixed T.
Cv is molar heat capacity at constant volume.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas both second derivatives are zero, so C<sub>P</sub> and C<sub>V</sub> depend only on T. For a real gas or liquid they drift with pressure or volume.
A common use is checking whether tabulated Cp at 1 bar can be used at 50 bar; integrate the pressure derivative.

examples.question: Liquid water at 300 K and 1 bar has v = 18.08 × 10⁻⁶ m³ mol⁻¹, α = 2.75 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and κ<sub>T</sub> = 4.51 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹ (IAPWS values). Calculate C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub>, and γ given C<sub>P</sub> = 75.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps: Write the relation: C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = T v α²/κ<sub>T</sub>.
Divide by κ<sub>T</sub>: 4.1019 × 10⁻¹⁰/4.51 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 0.910 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Pa·m³ = J).
Check: IAPWS gives C<sub>V</sub> = 74.41 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ directly. For a liquid the two heat capacities differ by about 1 %, so either may be used in rough heat balances.
examples.answer: C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = 0.910 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and γ = 1.012 for liquid water at 300 K.

examples.question: Treat CO<sub>2</sub> at 300 K and V = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³/mol as a van der Waals gas (a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻², b = 4.267 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol). Find C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> from C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = −T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>²/(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> and compare with R.
steps: That is 11.35/8.314 = 1.37 R. Attraction (the a term) makes the gas easier to compress, so (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> is smaller in size and the difference grows above R.

Check: an accurate equation of state for CO<sub>2</sub> at this state gives C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = 14.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; the van der Waals model gets the direction right but only about three quarters of the size.
examples.answer: C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = 11.35 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 1.37 R (accurate value 14.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

traps: Using Cp − Cv = R for a liquid. R applies only to an ideal gas.
Mixing mass volume with molar volume; v must be m³ mol⁻¹.
Getting the sign of α or κ<sub>T</sub> wrong; κ<sub>T</sub> is defined with a minus sign.
Forgetting to square α, or using T in °C instead of kelvin.
Using v in cm³ mol⁻¹ without converting to m³ mol⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why is C<sub>P</sub> greater than C<sub>V</sub> for a real gas?
quiz.a: At constant pressure the gas expands as it warms: it does work on the surroundings and, for a real gas, its internal energy also rises as the molecules move apart against their attraction. Both need extra heat for the same temperature rise.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas show Cp − Cv = R using α = 1/T and κ<sub>T</sub> = 1/P.
quiz.a: T v (1/T²)/(1/P) = vP/T = R because v = RT/P.

quiz.q: A liquid has α = 0 and finite κ<sub>T</sub>. What is Cp − Cv?
quiz.a: Zero, because the formula contains α²; no thermal expansion means no extra expansion work.

quiz.q: If v doubles while α and κ<sub>T</sub> stay fixed, what happens to Cp − Cv?
quiz.a: It doubles, because Cp − Cv is proportional to v.

quiz.q: What does (∂Cp/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = 0 mean for an ideal gas?
quiz.a: Cp does not change with pressure at fixed T; it depends only on T.

quiz.q: Why is γ = C<sub>P</sub>/C<sub>V</sub> never less than 1 for a stable phase?
quiz.a: C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = Tvα²/κ<sub>T</sub>. A stable phase has κ<sub>T</sub> > 0 (it shrinks when squeezed), and T, v and α² are never negative, so C<sub>P</sub> ≥ C<sub>V</sub> and γ ≥ 1, with γ = 1 only when α = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam.
